newsitem.title: UK: IEA sees six mbpd non-OPEC oil output surge by 2000.
newsitem.headline: IEA sees six mbpd non-OPEC oil output surge by 2000.

text.p: New upstream technology will drive non-OPEC oil supplies up 15 percent in five years to 2000 and leave oil-consuming nations much less reliant on Middle East supplies than previously expected, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday.
Non-OPEC supplies should hit 48.7 million barrels per day (bpd) by 2000, up 6.3 million from 42.4 million bpd in 1995, the West's Paris-based energy watchdog said in a new study.
The surge would compare with non-OPEC output growth of just 500,000 bpd from 41.9 million bpd in the five years from 1990.
"The revolution in upstream oil technology and practices that has been occurring over the last decade has fundamentally changed the medium-term outlook for the world oil market," the IEA said.

"Declining costs and increasing effectiveness are overturning the previous consensus of imminent non-OEPC supply declines in the face of rapidly rising demand, with the associated sharply increasing dependence on supplies from a few large producers in the Middle East," it added.
The agency said new offshore oilfields in the North Sea, not previously accessible or economic, were at the heart of upstream developments.

Upward trends in offshore production would continue at least into the first part of the next decade as the new technology spreads to the Gulf of Mexico, South America, West Africa, East Asia and elsewhere, the IEA study said.
Changes in fiscal regimes and new organisational approaches to the management of projects were also significant factors in the upstream oil outlook.

On the technological front, 3D and 4D seismic evaluations, horizontal drilling, sub-sea completions, multi-phase pipelines and floating production storage units and offshore loading vessels had greatly improved exploration and lowered development costs.
